source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Respect informed refusal, document capacity and risks, and provide the safest feasible follow-up plan","B":"Physically detain the capable adult solely because the healthcare team believes leaving is unsafe","C":"Assume the decision to leave automatically proves lack of capacity and permits involuntary detention","D":"Use a signed AMA form as the only required step and omit discussion of risks and alternatives"}}
source_row.rationale: A capable adult can refuse recommended treatment even when clinicians consider the choice unsafe. Informed refusal is a process rather than merely a signature: assess capacity, explain risks, benefits and alternatives, document the discussion, and reduce harm through a safe-as-feasible discharge/follow-up plan. Facility policy and applicable law still apply.
source_row.source_detail: AMA ethics discussion: adults with decision-making capacity may refuse treatment; holding a capable patient may constitute false imprisonment. Informed refusal requires capacity assessment, information about consequences, and documentation rather than relying only on an AMA form.
source_row.source_name: AMA Journal of Ethics — Ethically Informed Discharge Planning and Informed Refusal
source_row.stem: An adult with decision-making capacity understands the recommended inpatient treatment and its risks but insists on leaving the hospital. What is the best response?
